title: An ordinary day: the present tense
goal: Describe your daily routine in the present tense — one ending for every verb — and put words like *alltid*, *ofte* and *aldri* in the right place.
bekal: form the present tense by swapping *å* for the ending **-r**
recognize the seven short verbs whose present tense is irregular
put *alltid*, *ofte*, *aldri*, *bare* in the same box as *ikke*
wave: Go back over **Unit 5** first: cover the Norwegian, look at the English translation, and rebuild the dialogue. Test the plurals — which take *-er*, which don't change, which change their vowel?

dialogs.title: Dialogue — En vanlig tirsdag
dialogs.intro: Ingrid is making tea. Budi has just come home and drops into a chair, looking exhausted.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Du ser trøtt ut. Hva gjør du hver dag, egentlig?
lines.id: You look tired. What do you actually do every day?
lines.literal: you look tired out. what do you every day, actually?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeg våkner klokka seks. Så dusjer jeg og spiser frokost.
lines.id: I wake up at six. Then I shower and have breakfast.
lines.literal: I wake the-clock six. then shower I and eat breakfast.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nesten alltid. Så tar jeg bussen til universitetet.
lines.id: Almost always. Then I take the bus to the university.
lines.literal: almost always. then take I the-bus to the-university.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeg leser på biblioteket til fire. Der er det stille.
lines.id: I study at the library until four. It's quiet there.
lines.literal: I read at the-library until four. there is it quiet.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jo, jeg svømmer av og til. Men jeg går ofte tur i stedet.
lines.id: I do — I swim now and then. But I often go for a walk instead.
lines.literal: yes, I swim off and to. but I go often walk in the-place.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Det er veldig norsk. Vi går tur i all slags vær.
lines.id: That's very Norwegian. We go for walks in all kinds of weather.
lines.literal: that is very Norwegian. we go walk in all kinds weather.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeg vet. Dere sier at det ikke finnes dårlig vær.
lines.id: I know. You say there's no such thing as bad weather.
lines.literal: I know. you-all say that it not exists bad weather.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Bare dårlige klær. Nå lager jeg middag. Blir du?
lines.id: Only bad clothes. Now I'm making dinner. Are you staying?
lines.literal: only bad clothes. now make I dinner. stay you?

notes: **The Norwegian present tense takes one move: drop *å*, add *-r*.** *å våkne* → *våkner*, *å dusje* → *dusjer*, *å svømme* → *svømmer*. And as you've seen since Unit 1, that form is **the same for everyone** — nothing changes according to the subject.
**Verbs that already end in a vowel just add -r**: *å gå* → *går*, *å se* → *ser*, *å bo* → *bor*, *å ha* → *har*, *å få* → *får*. A short group, but used constantly.

**Spiser du alltid frokost?** — notice *alltid* stands in the same box as *ikke*: after the verb and the subject. The whole family — *alltid*, *ofte*, *aldri*, *sjelden*, *bare*, *også*, *kanskje* — uses the same box.
**Trener du aldri?** is answered with *jo*, not *ja*, because the question contains a negative (*aldri*). This is the *jo* from Unit 2, now in its natural habitat.

**Å gå tur** means "to go for a walk", and it's one of the most Norwegian expressions there is. Notice *tur* stands **bare**, with no article — part of a group of fixed expressions like *på jobb*, *til fots*, *i seng*.
**Det finnes** means "there is, there exists", and its form never changes. It's a relative of *det er*, but feels firmer: *det finnes ikke dårlig vær* — there's no such thing as bad weather.

grammars.title: The infinitive and the present tense
body: The Norwegian infinitive is always preceded by **å** (said **oh**), which works exactly like English *to*. Dictionaries list verbs in this form.
after: The present tense covers **three** things that English keeps apart: habits (*jeg leser hver dag* — I read every day), what's happening now (*jeg leser nå* — I'm reading now), and what's going to happen (*jeg reiser i morgen* — I'm leaving tomorrow). One form for all three.

So **don't look for an equivalent of "am …-ing"**. *Jeg spiser* already means "I'm eating" when the situation calls for it. If you really want to stress it, add *akkurat nå* (right now) or use *holder på å* (*jeg holder på å spise*), but that's rarely needed at A1.

grammars.title: Seven irregular verbs
body: Norwegian has almost no irregular verbs in the present tense — these seven are practically the whole list, and they're all words you use every day.
after: The only rows you really have to learn are the first four: **er, gjør, sier, vet**. The rest just adjust their spelling and still end in *-r*.
Compare that with French, which has dozens of irregular verbs with six forms each, or Spanish with three conjugation groups. Norwegian hands you four words and you're done.
⚠️ The helper verbs (*kan*, *vil*, *skal*, *må*, *bør*) **don't end in -r at all** in the present tense. They're not irregular but a group of their own, and the next unit is all about them.

grammars.title: The fourth box: where alltid, ofte, aldri go
body: Remember the five-box frame from Unit 3? The fourth box — where *ikke* sits — actually belongs to a bigger family of words. All its members use the same box.
after: The most frequent members of the fourth box: **ikke** (not), **alltid** (always), **ofte** (often), **aldri** (never), **sjelden** (rarely), **bare** (only), **også** (also), **kanskje** (maybe), **nok** (probably), **jo** (after all, you know), **allerede** (already).

⚠️ Note the difference from English: "I **always eat** breakfast" puts *always* before the verb, but Norwegian puts it after: *jeg spiser **alltid** frokost*. And *aldri* already contains the negative, so **don't add *ikke***: *Jeg spiser aldri frokost* — not *jeg spiser ikke aldri* (think "I don't never").

blocks.text: Read this list aloud as one story, from morning to evening. These are the sentences you'll need most when people ask *hva gjør du?*

head: Norsk
English
rows: Jeg står opp med en gang.
I shower and brush my teeth.
Jeg spiser frokost og drikker te.
I have breakfast and drink tea.
I take the bus to work.
Jeg begynner å jobbe klokka åtte.

blocks.text: Two more everyday sentences hide something we haven't covered yet. *Jeg ser **på** TV* (I watch TV) needs a fixed preposition — without *på* the sentence is wrong. And *jeg legger **meg*** (I go to bed) uses a reflexive pronoun, because it literally means "I lay myself down". Verbs like these are waiting in Unit 18; for now learn those two sentences whole.

blocks.title: A quick self-test
items: Describe your day yesterday — sorry, **today** — in ten sentences in a row, out loud. All in the present tense; the past tense only arrives in Unit 15.
Then repeat the whole thing, slipping one word from the list above into every sentence. If one lands in the wrong place, go back to the fourth-box table.
Final test: negate five sentences in one go. *Jeg spiser aldri frokost. Jeg tar sjelden bussen.* Notice the box stays the same.
